St. Gregory Palamas

St. Gregory Palamas

Period
1296–1359 (source account)
Region
Balkans
Titles / vocation
Hierarch · Monastic · Church Father
Commemoration
November 14

Introduction

St. Gregory is remembered as archbishop of Thessalonica and a defender of hesychast theology. The OCA life traces his movement from Constantinople to Athos, the controversies surrounding his teaching, and his episcopal ministry. It records his repose in 1359 and canonization in 1368. The profile connects his life with further reading while distinguishing biography from the detailed arguments of his writings.

Read circumstances and sources

Background

The ACROD biographical article places Gregory in a wealthy Constantinopolitan family known at the imperial court. His education and prospects could have led to government service, but he went to Mount Athos and trained under experienced monastic guides. It records movement to Thessalonica in 1326 under the threat of a Turkish attack, ordination to the priesthood, a later return to Athos, and service as abbot of Esphigmenou. This background helps explain why his later theological work was closely connected with Athonite monastic life rather than being only an academic dispute.

[2] Official ecclesiastical biography or biographical address · Biographical reading / named life section

Life and notable events

The OCA Life describes conflict with Barlaam, Akyndinos and Patriarch John Kalekas, imprisonment, release in 1347, and election for Thessalonica. Opposition delayed his entry. Later captured at sea by the Turks, he remained a prisoner about a year before ransom, teaching Christian prisoners and captors during that period.

[1] Ecclesiastical saint’s life · Published life; biographical narrative and concluding account

Death and martyrdom

After release St. Gregory returned to Thessalonica. The Life dates his repose to November 14, 1359 and formal glorification to 1368 under Philotheus. Its vision of Chrysostom and final words are hagiographic details.

[1] Ecclesiastical saint’s life · Published life; biographical narrative and concluding account

Writings and legacy

GOARCH connects his public work with the councils of 1341 and 1347 and his defense of the distinction between God’s unapproachable essence and uncreated energies. The question concerned whether genuine communion with God is possible, not merely the use of a particular word for light. His subsequent liturgical memory includes November 14 and the second Sunday of Great Lent. These commemorations connect the remembered life, its controversies, and its later reception in Orthodox worship.

[3] Official ecclesiastical biography or biographical address · Biographical reading / named life section

Father Pehanich connects Palamas’s teaching with Basil’s Letter 234. The following passage is Basil’s own wording in Blomfield Jackson’s historical English translation; it is background to Palamas, not a quotation from Palamas.

[2] Official ecclesiastical biography or biographical address · Biographical reading / named life section

For they confess themselves that there is a distinction between the essence and each one of the attributes enumerated. The operations are various, and the essence simple, but we say that we know our God from His operations, but do not undertake to approach near to His essence. His operations come down to us, but His essence remains beyond our reach.

[4] Patristic theological letter · Letter CCXXXIV, section 1; closing sentences beginning “For they confess themselves”
